name: Liftoff
summary: Liftoff runs a strength-ranking system, Bronze through Diamond, assigned first from a self-reported rep count during onboarding and then extended by logged workouts. Daily, weekly and one-time quests pay a currency called eggs, which doubles as both an earned and a purchasable balance spent on consumables and cosmetics. A predicted date for reaching the next rank tier, a seven-day trial, and a same-day exit offer all sit on top of the same ranking system before the user has completed a single workout. Leagues, leaderboards and a Pro subscription then extend the ranking comparison to other users.
teaser: Liftoff's exit offer promises "78% off forever" on a discount that actually runs about 50%.

observations.name: Language choice at launch
observations.observed: On first launch, Liftoff shows a front screen with a Get Started button and an option to sign into an existing account, along with an immediate language choice offering ten languages.

observations.name: Introductory slider
observations.observed: After Get Started, Liftoff shows a four-part slider with Skip and Next controls. The slides cover reaching fitness goals by climbing ranks, analyzing the body's potential, a personalized workout plan, and Liftoff as an all-in-one fitness companion, ending on a Let's Go button.

observations.name: Guided questionnaire host
observations.observed: After Let's Go, an animated character named Jimbo introduces the questionnaire that follows, with a progress bar running along the top of each screen and answers chosen from button options. The progress bar covers a required flow rather than an optional set of attributes.

observations.name: Experience level question
observations.observed: The first question asks how experienced the user is with working out, offering never worked out, beginner, intermediate or advanced.

observations.name: Top fitness goal question
observations.observed: Liftoff asks for the user's top fitness goal, offering becoming stronger, losing weight, building muscle, an option framed around ranks, and becoming more consistent.

observations.name: Goal-matched reassurance screen
observations.observed: After the goal question, Liftoff shows a screen reading that the user is in the right place, with copy that changes depending on the goal chosen. Two of the goals also show a five-star review matching that goal. The rank-option screen frames Liftoff as the way to step into ranked lifting, without a review shown alongside it.

observations.name: Restarting the questionnaire
observations.observed: Going back from the reassurance screen opens a warning that the user will return to the landing page and lose progress. Taking that route restarts the whole questionnaire from its first question, with the goal options appearing in a different order on the restart.

observations.name: Acquisition source question
observations.observed: After the reassurance screen, Liftoff asks how the user came to hear of it, offering friends or family, TikTok, Instagram, Facebook, YouTube, Snapchat, the App Store, or another source.

observations.name: Body information and age
observations.observed: Under a basic-info heading, Liftoff asks for sex, height, weight and age on separate screens. Sex is chosen between two illustrated characters that change pose with a thumbs up once picked. Height is set on a fast vertical slider and shown in centimeters, while weight is then asked in pounds. The age selector runs from 13 to 120.

observations.name: Avatar introduction and selection
observations.observed: Liftoff introduces an avatar through a short sequence of copy describing it as a reflection of the user that grows and celebrates wins, then asks the user to pick one of six starting avatars of different ethnicities and ages, stating it can be personalized later.

tags.name: Cosmetic Customization
tags.confidence: O40 and O45 (tier: strongly supported, the items and the avatar editor are offered, but applying a cosmetic is not observed).
confidences: O40 and O45 (tier: strongly supported, the items and the avatar editor are offered, but applying a cosmetic is not observed).
tags.rationale: Liftoff sells profile banners, several border types and several app theme types as store content, which places them on the content side of the library's boundary with built-in settings (tier: directly observed). The profile offers further avatar editing after the onboarding pick, which promised "We'll personalize it later" (tier: directly observed). No cosmetic changes a capability on the observed evidence (tier: strongly supported). The structure corresponds to the Identity Expression pattern (tier: strongly supported).

For level borders, a presentation tied only to level would be a status indicator rather than a cosmetic, and a session applying one would settle it.

observations.name: Profiling questions
observations.observed: Liftoff asks further questions about mindset, sensitive areas and energy during workouts: how often the user thinks about getting in shape, whether they struggle with a sensitive back, knees, shoulders or wrists, and how their energy levels run during workouts.

observations.name: Relate-to-statement screens
observations.observed: Liftoff shows three screens each asking whether the user relates to a single first-person statement: that progress is hard to notice, that they don't know which body part needs work, and that they don't push themselves hard enough.

observations.name: Problem screens
observations.observed: After the statements, Liftoff shows three screens naming a difficulty, invisible progress, blind spots from not knowing which muscle is lagging, and motivation not lasting, each with an illustrated character in a struggling pose, followed by a screen presenting Liftoff ranks as the path to getting stronger. The first problem screen names the same progress difficulty regardless of which statement the user had related to.

observations.name: Workout plan and equipment
observations.observed: Liftoff asks whether the user has a workout plan, then where they exercise: a large commercial gym, a small gym, a garage gym, or body weight only. Choosing a large commercial gym opens an equipment list with everything preselected; choosing body weight only opens the same list with nothing selected, while dozens of weights and machines stay listed regardless.

observations.name: Workout length and frequency
observations.observed: Liftoff asks which muscles were worked last, how long a typical workout lasts, and how many times a week the user works out, with the frequency answer receiving an evaluative label such as good, great, incredible, outstanding or unstoppable depending on the number of days chosen.

observations.name: First rank assessment
observations.observed: After stating that Liftoff has everything it needs for a first rank, it asks for the user's best lift, taking an exercise and a rep count. The user is offered push ups, pull ups, bench press, deadlift or squat, and can enter a rep count for one. Liftoff takes an exercise and a rep count for the first rank test; the exercise chosen appears as pull ups, and the loaded result names the exercise as push ups, with a rank of Bronze 3 and a stated top 76.23 percent.

tags.rationale: Liftoff assigns each ranked exercise, and each muscle in the body rank, a current state within an ordered series named Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum and Diamond, with numbered steps such as Bronze 3 (tier: directly observed). The state is assessed from performance: a self-reported rep count in O16 and logged sets in O33 (tier: directly observed). Movement between states was not observed. The product frames it through the path-to-Diamond screen in O19 and the predicted date in O17 (tier: directly observed). Under the presence standard, the ordered states, the assigned current state and the product's framing of advancement establish the label, and the reassessment rule is recorded as not observed. Liftoff names its own target obstacle in O13 ("Progress feels invisible"), which is stated product intent and not evidence that users meet that obstacle (tier: directly observed). The structure corresponds to the Visible Progress pattern (tier: strongly supported). The account level in O34 is a separate track, recorded at a lower tier.
tags.alternativeConsidered: Comparative Rank, because O16 pairs the tier with a percentile (tier: directly observed). That entry excludes a percentile without an assigned position, and no position was shown, so it is not applied. The two entries are not exclusive siblings. A session showing a tier change while the user's own result stays the same would show the tiers depend on other users, and Comparative Rank would then apply alongside Leveling.

No assumption behind the date, such as a training frequency or rate of improvement, is stated, and the prediction is not shown again later.

observations.name: Apple Health connection request
observations.observed: After the paywall and its exit offer close, Liftoff asks to connect Apple Health, recommending the user turn on every category, and states that fitness data will stay securely stored on the device. Every category in the system permission sheet starts switched off.

observations.name: Account creation and welcome
observations.observed: Liftoff asks the user to sign up to save their profile, offering sign up with Apple, sign up with Google, or continue with email, then greets the new account by a generated username combining the account holder's first name and a number. Jimbo celebrates the created profile before a Strava link prompt appears ahead of the main app opening.

observations.name: First home screen
observations.observed: The first unguided screen is Home, holding a six-item bottom menu for Home, Workout, Ranks, Nutrition, Friends and Profile, a header with the avatar, a flame, a number beside a blue icon, and a bell, three feeds, a prompt to unlock body rank progress for free, a getting-started section, a goal section, a last-14-workouts overview, and a discover section listing a leaderboard, a social feed, a streak calendar and a workout generator.

observations.name: Welcome quests
observations.observed: The Home getting-started section shows welcome quests framed as wrapping up the first day on Liftoff to earn a special reward, listing adding the Liftoff widget to the home screen and completing a first workout as the two tasks. The reward itself is not identified.

observations.name: Workout tab entry points
observations.observed: The Workout tab offers a daily workout, custom workout generation, saved routines and an empty workout. Today's workout was Chest and shoulders, 12 sets, 45 minutes. A workout generator also appears on Home under discover.

observations.name: Workout preview
observations.observed: Before a workout starts, Liftoff shows its duration, a level, the equipment used, recovered muscles, targeted muscles with percentages, and the exercise list, with knee push ups, wall push ups, body weight military press and knee pike push ups listed for this workout. The workout can be started directly from the preview.

observations.name: Logging a workout
observations.observed: During a workout, the user taps a check mark to complete each set while a timer runs, and a rest countdown of one and a half minutes starts once an exercise is completed. Liftoff reminds the user to rest between sets, additional sets can be added to an exercise, and the timer keeps counting through the whole workout.

observations.name: Posting a finished workout
observations.observed: Finishing a workout opens a posting surface where the user can add a photo and caption, choose consumables, tag friends, and post to Discovery and to Strava, showing which muscles were trained before asking whether the user is ready to finish and post. Consumables can also be chosen before the workout starts.

observations.name: Nutrition logging
observations.observed: The Nutrition tab lets the user log meals, including by photo, against a calorie goal, showing calories eaten and calories burned through exercise. Meal categories are Breakfast, Lunch, Dinner, Snack and Uncategorized. Logging a meal by photo is available without payment, while macros for protein, carbs and fat are held for Liftoff Pro.

observations.name: Training history displays
observations.observed: Liftoff shows the user's own training history in three places: a last-14-workouts overview on Home showing volume, duration, calories burned and body weight pulled from Apple Health; a memories calendar showing the avatar on a date with how much was exercised; and a health log showing changes in body weight, height and other measures. None of these displays asks for a response from the user.

observations.name: Strength rank ladder
observations.observed: Liftoff ranks strength per exercise and per muscle on an ordered ladder of Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum and Diamond, with numbered steps inside a tier such as Bronze 3. The Ranks tab gathers the user's rank, a body graph, leagues, a gallery, a calculator and analysis. The first rank comes from a self-reported rep count during onboarding, and a percentile accompanied that first result. The body rank is framed as showing how strong each muscle is, with the user directed to target lower-ranked muscles.

systemView: Liftoff is a complex system whose spine is the rank a user is assigned: the onboarding assessment sets the first rank, logged workouts and quests keep extending it, and that same ranking measure gates league access, frames the paywall, and anchors the leaderboards and social comparisons built on top of it.

mechanicWriteups.name: Leveling
mechanicWriteups.summary: Liftoff assigns a Bronze-to-Diamond rank per exercise and per muscle, first from a self-reported number, then from logged sets.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Liftoff places every ranked exercise, and every muscle in the body rank, on an ordered ladder running Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum and Diamond, with numbered steps inside a tier such as Bronze 3. The first rank comes from a rep count the user reports during onboarding for one chosen exercise; further exercises gain a rank once a workout logs sets against them. Liftoff also shows a level with a progress bar beside the avatar on the home screen.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The rank ladder is explained across dedicated onboarding screens before the first workout, then lives in the Ranks tab alongside a body graph, leagues, a gallery, a calculator and analysis. The account level sits fixed at the top of the home screen, next to the avatar.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff frames the rank ladder as the thing to act on, telling the user to target lower-ranked muscles to get stronger, and stages a screen showing the path all the way to Diamond before any workout is logged. The account level beside the avatar runs alongside the rank ladder without stating its own number, threshold, or what makes it move; the store's level borders are the only other place a level number could show up, and none is shown there either.
findings: The rank ladder runs Bronze, Silver, Gold, Platinum, Diamond, with numbered steps inside a tier.
The first rank comes from a self-reported rep count during onboarding.
Further exercises gain a rank once a workout logs sets against them.
A level and a progress bar sit beside the avatar on the home screen, with no number stated.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the rank ladder explanation screen naming all five tiers, and the account level beside the avatar.

mechanicWriteups.name: Experience Points
mechanicWriteups.summary: Claiming a quest or finishing a workout pays experience toward the level beside the avatar, with no amount ever shown.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Liftoff states that claiming a quest grants experience points, and a store item, the Double XP Shake, is described as doubling experience gained during a workout. Both routes feed the same level shown with a progress bar beside the avatar on the home screen.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Experience isn't shown as its own balance anywhere; it surfaces only through the copy on quest claims and the shake's own description, and through the level progress bar it's presumed to advance.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff never shows an experience amount, a level threshold, or a level changing, so what's confirmed is that two routes pay into the same value, not how much either one pays or what crossing a level actually does. The shake's claim to double the gain from a workout has nothing to double against, since no workout's own experience payout is ever shown either.
findings: Claiming a quest grants experience points.
The Double XP Shake doubles experience gained during a workout.
Both routes feed the level shown beside the avatar.
No experience amount, threshold, or level change is shown at any point.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: a quest claim stating its experience reward, and the Double XP Shake's item description.

mechanicWriteups.name: Achievement
mechanicWriteups.summary: Liftoff keeps a medal collection on the profile, some with hidden criteria, and lets the user pin three.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Profile holds a set of medals the user can collect, with some medals carrying criteria that stay hidden until met. The user can choose up to three medals to display on the profile.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Medals sit on the Profile tab as their own collection, separate from the badges awarded per exercise after a workout, with a display slot for three chosen medals.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff builds real suspense into part of the medal set by hiding what earns them, but nothing shown says whether the account already holds any medal, what a medal's criterion looks like once revealed, or what happens on attainment. The display slot for three medals is the only part of the mechanic actually demonstrated.
findings: Medals sit on the profile as their own collection.
Some medals have hidden criteria.
The user can choose up to three medals to display.
No medal attainment, criterion, or count is shown.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the medal collection screen, and the three-medal display slot on the profile.

mechanicWriteups.name: Daily / Weekly Quests
mechanicWriteups.summary: Profile lists separate daily, weekly and referral quests, each claimed for eggs and experience.
mechanicWriteups.observed: A quests surface on Profile groups tasks into daily quests, weekly quests and referral quests, including a quest to start a streak. Claiming a completed quest grants eggs and experience points.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The three quest groups sit together on one surface reached from Profile, with a claim action attached to each completed task.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff names three separate cadences on one screen but doesn't show any individual quest's task, target, or reward amount, and doesn't show whether the set refreshes on a boundary or what a referral quest actually asks the introduced person to do.
findings: Quests are grouped into daily, weekly and referral quests.
One quest asks the user to start a streak.
Claiming a quest grants eggs and experience points.
No individual quest's task, target, or reward amount is shown.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the quests surface showing all three groups.

mechanicWriteups.name: Challenge
mechanicWriteups.summary: A first-day objective pairs adding the home screen widget with completing one workout for an unnamed reward.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Liftoff sets a first-day objective, framed as wrapping up the first day on Liftoff to earn a special reward, with two tasks: adding the Liftoff widget to the home screen and completing a first workout.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The objective appears in a "Getting started" section on the home screen, listing both tasks together under the promised reward.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff names the reward only as special, never disclosing what it is, and nothing shown says what happens if the first day passes without both tasks done. The widget task is also asked for on its own screen earlier in onboarding, so the objective repeats a step the user may have already completed before it's even framed as a task.
findings: The objective is framed as wrapping up the first day on Liftoff.
Its two tasks are adding the home screen widget and completing a first workout.
The reward is named only as special, never identified.
The widget task is also requested earlier in onboarding, on its own.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the "Getting started" section showing both tasks and the reward line.

mechanicWriteups.name: Streak
mechanicWriteups.summary: A flame count of one sits atop the home screen, next to store items sold to restore a broken streak.
mechanicWriteups.observed: The home screen header shows a flame with a count of 1. Liftoff sells streak restorers in the store, described as being for when a user wants to restore their streak, and other users' streaks appear on their posts in Discovery.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The flame sits in the header at the top of the home screen, visible on every visit; the restorers are a separate line item in the store, and a quest task offers to start a streak.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Selling a restorer is Liftoff's own admission that the count can break, since nothing needs restoring if it can't, but nothing shown states what activity the streak counts, what period it runs on, or what breaks it. The count of 1 could describe a single qualifying day or a single qualifying week; the app doesn't say which.
findings: The home header shows a flame with a count of 1.
Streak restorers are sold in the store.
Other users' streaks appear on their Discovery posts.
A quest task offers to start a streak.
The qualifying activity, period, and break rule are not stated.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the home header flame, and the streak restorer in the store.

mechanicWriteups.name: Soft Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: Completing a quest is the earned route into eggs, the balance the store also sells for real money.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Liftoff grants eggs for claiming a completed quest, on daily, weekly and referral cadences. The user held enough eggs from quests alone to buy a Double XP Shake in the store without any money purchase.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The egg grant appears as part of the same claim action that pays experience, on the quests surface reached from Profile; the store where eggs are spent has no separate label distinguishing quest-earned eggs from purchased ones.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Eggs work as one balance no matter how they arrive, quest-earned or bought outright, which is also covered under Hard Currency for the purchasable side of the same balance. Liftoff never shows a balance figure or a claim amount, so what a quest actually pays into the balance isn't shown, only that it pays something.
findings: Claiming a quest grants eggs, on daily, weekly and referral cadences.
Eggs earned from quests alone paid for a store purchase, with no money spent.
No claim amount or balance figure is ever shown.
The same balance is also sold directly for money.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: a quest claim showing the egg grant, and the store purchase made with quest-earned eggs.

mechanicWriteups.name: Hard Currency
mechanicWriteups.summary: The same eggs quests pay out are also sold directly in packages from $0.99 to $99.99.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Liftoff's store sells eggs for money in packages from 100 eggs for $0.99 up to 14,000 eggs for $99.99. The same eggs are spent on consumables, cosmetics and a 10-egg deal refresh in the same store.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The egg packages sit in the store as a direct purchase option, priced in real money, alongside the same spend surfaces that quest-earned eggs draw from.
mechanicWriteups.noting: The largest package gives noticeably more eggs per dollar than the smallest, about 140 against about 101, which rewards buying in bulk. Since quests pay into the identical balance a shopper can buy directly, Liftoff never has to show the two routes as different currencies, and it doesn't.
findings: Egg packages range from 100 eggs for $0.99 to 14,000 eggs for $99.99.
The largest package gives about 140 eggs per dollar against about 101 for the smallest.
Eggs bought for money spend in the same store as quest-earned eggs.
No separate balance or label distinguishes purchased eggs from earned ones.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the egg package store screen showing both ends of the price range.

mechanicWriteups.name: Reward Multiplier
mechanicWriteups.summary: A store item consumed during a workout doubles the experience that workout pays, bought with eggs.
mechanicWriteups.observed: The Double XP Shake is a store item, bought with eggs, described as doubling experience gained during a workout and consumed on use. It's chosen at the start or end of a workout, alongside other consumables, and lands in an inventory once bought.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The shake sits in the store's consumables section next to other XP shakes, with its doubling effect and one-time consumption stated directly in its own item description.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Everything the shake does happens to a number Liftoff never shows: no workout's experience payout is stated with or without the shake, so the doubling is a claim about a figure the app keeps invisible on both sides. The shake changes only that payout, not the workout itself, which is what separates it from a held item that changes what happens during play.
findings: The Double XP Shake is bought with eggs and consumed on use.
Its stated effect is doubling experience gained during a workout.
It's chosen at the start or end of a workout.
No experience amount is shown with or without the shake applied.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Double XP Shake's store listing and item description.

mechanicWriteups.name: Cosmetic Customization
mechanicWriteups.summary: Eggs buy profile banners, borders, and app themes, on top of an avatar editable after onboarding.
mechanicWriteups.observed: The store sells profile banners, several border types including cosmic, elemental and level borders, and several theme types including prismatic, color, special and seasonal themes, all priced in eggs. Profile also offers further avatar editing beyond the six starting options chosen during onboarding.
mechanicWriteups.presented: Cosmetics sit in the store as their own category, separate from consumables, while avatar editing is reached from Profile rather than the store.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff sells cosmetics rather than unlocking them through play; every border and theme listed sits behind an egg price, not a rank or level crossed. Level borders are the one item named after a progression measure, but nothing shown ties owning or wearing one to an actual level reached, so it reads as a themed store item rather than a status attached to progress.
findings: The store sells profile banners, several border types, and several theme types.
All listed cosmetics are priced in eggs.
Avatar editing continues on Profile after the initial onboarding choice.
Level borders are named after a progression measure but not shown tied to an actual level.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the store's cosmetics category listing borders and themes.

mechanicWriteups.name: Social Feed
mechanicWriteups.summary: Discovery streams other users' workout posts, avatars and streaks, alongside separate For You and Friends feeds.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Home carries three labeled feeds: For You, Friends and Discovery. Discovery shows posts from multiple users carrying images, avatars, workout durations and streaks, with a report control on each post. Finished workouts can be posted into Discovery from the workout-completion flow.
mechanicWriteups.presented: All three feeds sit on the home screen under their own labels; Discovery is the only one described beyond its name.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff runs three feeds side by side but only demonstrates one of them, so what For You and Friends actually surface, and what orders any of the three, stays unstated. The report control on Discovery posts is the one piece of moderation infrastructure shown anywhere in the social layer.
findings: Home carries three labeled feeds: For You, Friends and Discovery.
Discovery shows posts with images, avatars, workout durations and streaks.
Posts in Discovery carry a report control.
Finished workouts can be posted into Discovery.
For You and Friends are not described beyond their labels.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the Discovery feed, and the three-feed layout on Home.

mechanicWriteups.name: Leaderboard
mechanicWriteups.summary: Rank standings compare the user against friends and everyone globally, with a regional view held for Pro.
mechanicWriteups.observed: The Ranks area shows rank standings on leaderboards with a friends scope and a global scope, plus a regional scope held for Liftoff Pro. Friends leaderboards are also listed on the Friends tab.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The leaderboard scopes sit together in the Ranks area, with the regional scope opening a Pro prompt instead of a standing when tapped.
mechanicWriteups.noting: Liftoff shows that a comparison exists in three scopes without showing what it orders users by or where the user themselves lands in it; the rank ladder is the most likely candidate for the measure, but nothing on screen states it directly. Pro's regional scope is priced on access to a standing the free scopes never reveal either.
findings: Leaderboards run in friends, global and Pro-only regional scopes.
Friends leaderboards also appear on the Friends tab.
The measure the leaderboard orders by is not stated.
The user's own position on any leaderboard is not shown.
mechanicWriteups.screenshotsNote: the friends and global leaderboard scopes, and the regional scope's Pro prompt.

mechanicWriteups.name: Progression Gate
mechanicWriteups.summary: Ranked leagues stay closed until the user has ranked ten separate exercises through the app's own systems.
mechanicWriteups.observed: Liftoff states that ranked leagues require the user to rank 10 exercises, a count that advances through the onboarding assessment and through logged workouts. The requirement is stated inside the Ranks tab, where leagues are listed.
mechanicWriteups.presented: The 10-exercise requirement appears as a stated line inside the Ranks tab, next to the leagues it gates.
mechanicWriteups.noting: The gate's condition is built entirely from the same ranking activity the rest of the app already asks for: ranking an exercise once counts toward leagues whether it happened during onboarding or in a logged workout since. Nothing shown displays a running count toward the ten, so a user has no way to see how close they are without opening the gated leagues screen itself.
findings: Ranked leagues require ranking 10 exercises.
The count advances through the onboarding assessment and logged workouts.
The requirement is stated inside the Ranks tab.
No running count toward the ten is shown.

proposedTags.name: Predicted Goal Date
proposedTags.draftDefinition: A predicted goal date is a date the product states for when the user will reach a named target state that the product itself assigns and will recognize when reached, derived from inputs the user has just supplied and presented as a prediction with a rising visual from the present to that date.
proposedTags.conditions: A present state measured or self-reported during onboarding (O16). A named target state in an ordered structure the product maintains and assigns (O19, O32). Placement ahead of a subscription offer (O48), which in this session is a sequence property and not a condition the pattern is shown to need (tier: plausible).
proposedTags.whyNotCovered: Future Projection covers a computed state that the product never recognizes as reached, such as a position forty years out that lies outside the product's own accounting. Gold is a tier on the ladder Liftoff assigns (O32, O33) (tier: directly observed). Liftoff would recognize the user reaching it by assigning it (tier: strongly supported). O17 therefore falls outside Future Projection on that entry's defining clause, and widening the entry to admit it was considered and declined on 15 Sep 2026, because that clause is what separates it from a goal and from Milestone. Milestone requires the product to recognize a point when it is reached, which a date stated in advance does not do. Commitment requires the user to state future behavior. No other entry classifies a date the product states for reaching a target state it will itself recognize.
proposedTags.recurrenceElsewhere: The pattern can be described without reference to Liftoff: any product that measures a baseline during onboarding and holds an ordered target state it assigns can state a date for reaching it, as fitness, weight, learning and savings products do (tier: plausible, not drawn from the session).
proposedTags.caveat: Held open on 15 Sep 2026 rather than written as an entry. The distinction from Future Projection stands, but the evidence is thin where it matters. The narration reads out no assumption behind the date, which does not establish that none is on screen, and the graph's contents beyond a sharp rise were not captured (tier: unresolved). Either of two things would settle it: a Liftoff session that captures the prediction screen in full, including any assumption, figure or label on the graph, or a second app that states a date for a target state the product itself recognizes. The proposal stays open in Pass three until one of them is available.

system.tagline: A strength rank assigned in onboarding becomes the gate, the leaderboard measure, and the frame for every paywall that follows.
system.overview: Liftoff assigns a strength rank from a self-reported rep count before the first workout, then extends it through logged sets across a Bronze-to-Diamond ladder covering both exercises and muscles. Quests pay eggs and experience on daily, weekly and referral cadences, the same eggs the store also sells directly for money and spends on consumables, cosmetics and a deal refresh. A ten-exercise threshold gates ranked leagues, a flame counts a streak the store sells restorers for, and a predicted date for reaching the next rank tier appears before the paywall, a seven-day trial followed immediately by a same-day exit offer.
system.loop: Answer the onboarding questionnaire, report a rep count for one exercise, and receive a first rank with a percentile. See a predicted date for reaching the next tier, then the paywall and its exit offer. Log a workout, which produces exercise rank badges and counts toward the ten exercises ranked leagues require. Claim daily, weekly and referral quests for eggs and experience, spend eggs on consumables and cosmetics or save them for a bigger purchase, and buy eggs directly if not. Watch the account level rise beside the avatar, and check a flame count and leaderboards for how the ranking measure looks against other users.
system.keyInsight: Liftoff's economy and its progression system share almost nothing but a currency: eggs fund cosmetics, a deal refresh and the one item, the Double XP Shake, that feeds back into experience, while the rank ladder that gives the app its name advances purely through onboarding input and logged sets, untouched by anything eggs buy. The one place they meet, the shake's XP boost, doubles a number the app never discloses on either side of the purchase.
system.whatMakesItWork: Every currency route lands in the same undifferentiated balance, so Liftoff never has to explain why an egg from a quest spends differently than an egg bought for $99.99, because it doesn't. The rank ladder gets the same treatment from a different direction: it's assigned from the first onboarding answer, before the user has done anything the app could call training, which lets the predicted-date screen and the paywall both borrow the ladder's authority before there's any workout behind it.

connections.title: Ranking exercises is what leagues count toward
connections.desc: The ten-exercise requirement for ranked leagues counts the same ranking activity the rank ladder already tracks, whether an exercise was ranked during onboarding or through a logged workout.
connections.effect: Nothing new has to happen for the gate to open; whatever the user already does to build their rank ladder is also progress toward leagues.

connections.title: Claiming a quest is how eggs are earned
connections.desc: Every quest claim, on a daily, weekly or referral cadence, pays eggs into the same balance the store spends.
connections.effect: The quest surface is the app's only shown non-purchase route into the currency, so returning to claim quests is also the free way to afford the store.

connections.title: The same claim also pays experience
connections.desc: A quest claim grants eggs and experience points together, in the same action.
connections.effect: A user checking quests for eggs is banking experience at the same time, without a separate decision to do so.

connections.title: Experience feeds the level beside the avatar
connections.desc: Workouts and quests both grant experience, and Liftoff shows that experience toward the account level displayed with a progress bar next to the avatar.
connections.effect: The account level reads as the sum of everything the user has already done for other reasons, not a track pursued on its own.

connections.title: One balance carries both currency labels
connections.desc: The eggs a quest pays out and the eggs sold for money spend in the exact same store, with no separate balance or label distinguishing where a given egg came from.
connections.effect: A player who never pays can still reach anything in the store, purely on quest income, since Liftoff draws no line between an earned egg and a bought one.

connections.title: Quest-earned eggs bought the multiplier
connections.desc: The Double XP Shake was bought with eggs the user had earned from quests alone, without any money purchase.
connections.effect: The shake's doubling effect is reachable through play, not gated behind spending real money, as long as the user keeps claiming quests.

connections.title: The shake doubles a number that's never shown
connections.desc: The Double XP Shake is described as doubling experience gained during a workout, the same experience value that otherwise feeds the account level with no amount ever stated.
connections.effect: The shake's whole pitch rests on a figure the app never discloses on either side, so its actual value to the level beside the avatar can't be checked against what a workout would have paid without it.

connections.title: A quest exists just to start the streak
connections.desc: One of the listed quests specifically asks the user to start a streak, the same flame count shown at the top of the home screen.
connections.effect: The streak isn't only a passive count the app happens to track; it's also something the quest surface actively directs the user toward beginning.

connections.title: Every cosmetic is priced in the same currency
connections.desc: Profile banners, borders and app themes are all store items priced in eggs, the same balance sold directly for money in packages up to $99.99.
connections.effect: A cosmetic never has to be earned or unlocked; whoever buys enough eggs, however they got them, can own any of them.
